links.note: 891 calls not slighting the power of the able (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் இகழாமை) the head of all safeguards, போற்றலுள் எல்லாம் தலை. 444 uses the same closing formula, வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை, for living so that those greater than oneself become one's own. Read together, the same class of people is the object of both rules: winning them is the first of strengths, and not offending them the first of protections.

891 makes not slighting the able the chief safeguard; 861 tells the ruler to avoid standing against the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக). The chapter on enmity gives as a tactical rule what 891 gives as a rule of self-protection.

892 warns that going on without cherishing the great (பெரியாரைப் பேணாது ஒழுகின்) brings, through them, ills that do not leave. 976 says the intent to cherish and win the great (பெரியாரைப் பேணிக் கொள்வேம் என்னும் நோக்கு) is simply absent from the minds of the small. The shared verb பேணு ties them: 976 names who it is that fails to cherish, 892 what the failure costs.

892 says disregard of the great brings unending trouble (பேரா இடும்பை); 450 says letting go the tie with the good (நல்லார் தொடர் கைவிடல்) is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many. Both chapters on the great rank a bad relation to them above ordinary dangers, 450 by a number and 892 by permanence.

893 says: if you want ruin (கெடல்வேண்டின்), go ahead without listening and wrong those able to destroy. 922 says: do not drink, but if anyone will, let it be those who do not want the regard of the worthy (எண்ணப்பட வேண்டாதார்). Both forbid by an ironic permission addressed to whoever wants the bad result, once about offending the powerful and once about liquor.

893 states as irony what 861 states as a plain command: offending those with the power to destroy (அடல்வேண்டின் ஆற்றுபவர்) is a way to seek one's own ruin, and 861 says to avoid opposing the stronger (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக).

894 says the unable doing harm to the able (ஆற்றுவார்க்கு ஆற்றாதார் இன்னா செயல்) is like beckoning Death with the hand. 250 asks one about to go against someone weaker (மெலியார்மேல் செல்லுமிடத்து) to think of oneself before the stronger (வலியார்முன்). Both reason from the weak facing the strong: 894 uses it as prudence in the Book of Wealth, 250 turns the same experience into a ground for compassion in the Book of Virtue.

In 894 the weak who injure the strong call Death (கூற்றம்) over with their own hand. In 765 an army is defined by the power to stand together even if Death comes raging against it (கூற்றுடன்று மேல்வரினும்). The figure of Death serves opposite lessons: facing it is the army's merit when it comes unbidden, and folly when one has summoned it oneself.

895 says those who draw the anger of a king of fierce might (வெந்துப்பின் வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர்) cannot go on existing anywhere they go. 691 gives the working rule for those who serve such kings: like people warming at a fire, neither move off nor come close (அகலாது அணுகாது தீக்காய்வார் போல்க). 895 states the danger, and 691 the conduct that lives beside it.

895 makes the king's anger inescapable for those under him; 899 says that if those of exalted resolve flare up (ஏந்திய கொள்கையார் சீறின்), the king himself (வேந்தனும்) breaks midway and loses his kingship. Within the chapter the pair sets up an order of power: the king who destroys others can himself be destroyed by the anger of the great. Parimelazhagar takes வேந்தன் in 899 as Indra.

896: even one burned by fire may survive (உய்வுண்டாம்), but those who go on offending the great will not (உய்யார்). 110: those who destroy any good may find escape (உய்வுண்டாம்), but there is none (உய்வில்லை) for one who destroys a kindness done to him. The same formula of 'escape exists for X, none for Y' marks two offences the book treats as beyond remedy, ingratitude in the Book of Virtue and offence against the great in the Book of Wealth.

207 says those who incur any enmity whatever survive it (எனைப்பகை உற்றாரும் உய்வர்), and only the enmity of one's own evil deeds follows and kills. 896 says those who keep offending the great do not survive (உய்யார்). If எனைப்பகை is taken literally as every human enmity, the two conflict; the conflict eases if 207's phrase is read as a rhetorical foil for the enmity of deeds, or if the harm in 896 is understood as itself the fruit of a wrong deed.

896 sets fire, which one can survive, against offending the great, which one cannot. 129 sets the wound burned by fire, which heals within (உள்ளாறும்), against the scar burned by the tongue, which does not (ஆறாதே). Both use fire as the lesser, survivable harm in order to measure a harm that arises between people.

897 asks what a life excellent in every part and lofty wealth (வகைமாண்ட வாழ்க்கையும் வான்பொருளும்) come to if the worthy of great stature are angered (தக்கார் செறின்). 900 says even those with support beyond measure (இறந்தமைந்த சார்பு) do not survive if those of the highest distinction are angered (சீரார் செறின்). The two close on the same word செறின் and between them cancel a person's own assets and then his outside supports.

444 says living so that those greater than oneself become one's own is the head of all strengths (வன்மையுள் எல்லாம் தலை). 897 gives the other side: a fully appointed life and great wealth count for nothing (என்னாம்) once the worthy great are angered. Together they make one's standing with the great, and not one's possessions, the deciding strength.

898 calls the great hill-like (குன்றன்னார்) and says that if they will a man's lowering, those who seemed fixed on earth perish with their line (குடியொடு மாய்வர்). 29 speaks of those who have climbed and stand on the hill of good qualities (குணமென்னும் குன்றேறி நின்றார்), whose anger cannot be withstood even for a moment. The hill figure and the claim about their displeasure recur across the Book of Virtue and the Book of Wealth; Parimelazhagar takes both groups as ascetics.

898 plays on குன்று (hill) and குன்ற (to diminish): if the hill-like intend diminishment, the seemingly permanent vanish. 965 uses the same play: even the hill-like (குன்றின் அனையாரும்) will diminish (குன்றுவர்) if they do a lowering thing as small as a kunri seed. In 898 the hill-like bring others low; in 965 they themselves can be brought low by their own act, so height gives power over others but no protection from one's own lapse.

899 says that if those of exalted resolve flare up, even the king (வேந்தனும்) breaks midway and loses his rule; Parimelazhagar reads வேந்தன் here as Indra losing his station. 25 names Indra, king of those in the wide heaven (அகல்விசும்புளார் கோமான் இந்திரனே), as sufficient witness to the power of one who has quenched the five senses. On Parimelazhagar's reading both verses point to the same story of Indra and an ascetic, once to praise renouncers and once to warn rulers.

264 says that crushing foes (ஒன்னார்த் தெறல்) and raising friends come through austerity if the ascetic so intends (எண்ணின் தவத்தான் வரும்). 899 shows that power from the receiving side: when those of exalted resolve (ஏந்திய கொள்கையார்) are roused, a king loses his kingship. 264 states the capacity in the chapter on austerity; 899 draws the political consequence.

900 says that even those with support beyond measure will not survive (உய்யார்) if those of the highest distinction are angered (சிறந்தமைந்த சீரார் செறின்). 29 says the anger (வெகுளி) of those standing on the hill of good qualities is hard to ward off (காத்தல் அரிது) even for a moment. The Book of Wealth applies to kings and their resources what the opening chapters said in praise of renouncers.

303 says to forget anger toward anyone at all (யார்மாட்டும்), because every evil is born from it. 900 treats the anger of the most distinguished (சீரார் செறின்) as a force no support can save one from, and Parimelazhagar and Pope take these as people of great austerity. If they are ascetics, the chapter on not being angry would have them without anger; the conflict depends on that identification and on reading 900 as accepting such anger, where it may only be warning the offender of what follows.

901 says those who desire the wife (மனைவிழைவார்) do not reach the excellent fruit, and that this is what those who desire action do not want; the edition prints வினைவிழையார், but Parimelazhagar's gloss reads வினைவிழைவார். 615 has the same contrast in nearly the same words: one who does not desire pleasure and desires action (இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான்) is the pillar that holds up his kin. Both set வினை against pleasure, and 615 gives the positive figure of which 901 gives the failure.

45 says that when household life has love and virtue (அன்பும் அறனும்), these are its character and its fruit (பண்பும் பயனும்); Parimelazhagar takes the love as that owed to one's wife. 901 says those who fix their desire on the wife (மனைவிழைவார்) miss the excellent fruit (மாண்பயன்). The pair marks a line between love within the household, which is its fruit, and விழைவு that lets the wife rule the man, which loses it; Parimelazhagar reads 901 as men who follow the wife's lead for pleasure's sake.

no_link_reason: The verse's claim (the prosperity of a man who desires his woman without regard brings shame) is repeated only by its neighbours 903 and 907; I found no verse outside the chapter that adds to it.

links.note: 903 calls a man's stooping before his wife (இல்லாள்கண் தாழ்ந்த) இயல்பின்மை, something against the natural order, which shames him among the good. 55 praises the wife who rises worshipping her husband (கொழுநன் தொழுதெழுவாள்). The two show that the book fixes the direction of deference in marriage: it is a merit in the wife and a disgrace in the husband.

978 says greatness always bows (பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை), and elsewhere the book calls bowing good for everyone. 903 names one bowing that brings shame: lowering oneself before one's wife (தாழ்ந்த இயல்பின்மை), which Parimelazhagar explains as arising from fear. The pair separates humility that comes from the absence of pride from submission that comes from fear.

904 says the man who fears his wife gets no distinction from his command of action (வினையாண்மை வீறெய்தல் இன்று). 1026 defines good manliness (நல்லாண்மை) as making the mastery of one's house one's own (இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்), which Parimelazhagar takes as leading one's family. Both build on ஆண்மை as mastery: the man of 904 has given up mastery at home, and his mastery of work earns no honour.

904 denies வீறு (distinction) to the action of the wife-fearing man: வினையாண்மை வீறெய்தல் இன்று. 665 says the firmness in action (வினைத்திட்பம்) of those who have attained distinction (வீறெய்தி மாண்டார்) reaches the king and is held in regard. The same phrase வீறு எய்து names what capable action normally earns and what, in 904, fear of the wife withholds.

428 says fearing what should be feared (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல்) is the work of the wise and not fearing it is folly. 905 describes fear aimed at the wrong object: one who fears his wife (இல்லாளை அஞ்சுவான்) will always be afraid to do good to good people (நல்லார்க்கு நல்ல செயல்). The pair shows that the book judges fear by its object, and that misplaced fear blocks good action.

905 says the man who fears his wife fears to do good to the good; 908 says those who act as she wishes (பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகுபவர்) neither meet their friends' needs nor do good (நன்றாற்றார்). Both state the cost to others: the wife-ruled man fails the good in 905 and his friends in 908.

906 says that even if they live like the gods (இமையாரின் வாழினும்), men who fear their wife's bamboo-like shoulders (அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சுபவர்) have no dignity (பாடிலர்). In 1088 a lover exclaims that his might (பீடு), feared by enemies in battle, has broken before her bright forehead alone. Both show male standing giving way before a woman's bodily feature; the Book of Wealth counts it a disgrace, while in the Book of Love it is a lover's speech in the moment and carries no judgment.

1011 ranks shame at one's deeds (கருமத்தால் நாணுதல்) as true shame and sets aside the shame of fair-browed women (திருநுதல் நல்லவர் நாண்) as another kind. 907 says a woman who has shame (நாணுடைப் பெண்) has more greatness than the manhood of one who lives doing a woman's bidding. So the woman's modesty that 1011 treats as the lesser kind still outranks, in 907, manhood that has given up command.

907 gives greatness to the woman with shame over the submissive man's manhood (பெண்ணே பெருமை உடைத்து). 1137, a speech in the Book of Love, says nothing has more worth than womanhood that suffers a sea of desire and still does not mount the palmyra horse (மடலேறாப் பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்கது இல்). In both, a woman's restraint is measured against a man's lack of it and ranked higher.

907 pairs நாண் and ஆண்மை: manhood that obeys a woman is worth less than womanhood with shame. In 1134 a lover says the fierce flood of desire carries off the raft made of shame and good manliness (நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை). Both treat shame and manliness as the two things a man loses together under a woman's hold; 907 states it as a judgment, 1134 as a lover's own complaint.

788 defines friendship as removing a friend's distress on the spot (ஆங்கே இடுக்கண் களைவது), like the hand of a man whose garment slips. 908 says those who live as the woman of the fine brow wishes (நன்னுதலாள் பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகுபவர்) do not see their friends' needs through (நட்டார் குறைமுடியார்). 908 names a condition under which the duty of 788 goes unmet: the man's actions are no longer his own to direct.

908 describes men who live as the woman wishes, பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகுபவர்; 141 speaks of the folly of living in desire for another man's woman, பெட்டொழுகும் பேதைமை. The same pairing of பெட்டு (desire, wish) with ஒழுகு (to conduct oneself) describes a life steered by desire in both, in 141 the man's own desire for a forbidden woman and in 908 the wishes of his own wife.

760 says that for those who have made abundant wealth the other two, virtue and pleasure, are easily had together (ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு). 909 says that deeds of virtue, ample wealth and the other pursuits (அறவினையும் ஆன்ற பொருளும் பிறவினையும்) are all absent in those who do a woman's bidding; Parimelazhagar and Pope take பிறவினை as pleasure. Both use the three aims as the measure of a life: 760 shows how they are gained together, 909 a way they are lost together.

754 says wealth that comes by right means and without wrong yields virtue and also pleasure (அறன் ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும்). 909 lists the same three goods as missing in men who do a woman's bidding (பெண்ஏவல் செய்வார்கண் இல்). Where 754 treats the three as flowing from one sound source, 909 treats them as shut off by one fault.

910: the folly that comes of attachment to a woman (பெண்சேர்ந்தாம் பேதைமை) is never found in those whose hearts hold deliberation and firmness (எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சத்து இடனுடையார்க்கு ... இல்). 141: the folly of desiring another's wife (பெட்டொழுகும் பேதைமை) is not found in those who have seen virtue and wealth (அறம்பொருள் கண்டார்கண் இல்). Both chapters use the same sentence shape, calling the conduct பேதைமை and saying it is absent in people of understanding; they treat it as an error of judgment as much as a moral fault.

910 says those with deliberation and firmness of heart never fall into the folly of attachment to a woman. 917, in the next chapter, says it is those without a firm heart (நிறைநெஞ்சம் இல்லவர்) who touch the shoulders of women who embrace with their minds on other things. Both locate the safeguard in the man's own நெஞ்சம், stated positively in 910 for the wife-ruled man and negatively in 917 for the client of courtesans.
